title: The heavy letters inside words: ص ض ط ظ
objectives: Student can read fully-vocalised words containing ص ض ط ظ while sustaining tafkhīm through the whole letter, and can hear the heaviness in the neighbouring vowel rather than only in the consonant.
Student can distinguish ص from س, ض from د, ض from ظ, and ط from ت in real minimal pairs, and can self-test using سَا/صَا and ضِدّ without the teacher.
Student can produce qalqalah on a ط carrying sukūn while correctly HOLDING a ظ carrying sukūn — the contrast that proves the two heavy letters are not interchangeable.
Student can read وَلَا ٱلضَّآلِّينَ with a correct ض, a held shadda and a six-count madd, and can name what goes wrong when it is read as ٱلظَّالِّينَ.

slides.heading: Lesson 1.14 — The heavy letters inside words: ص ض ط ظ

audio.cue: Close the letter and stop. No extra vowel, no stretching.
ط is one of the five قطب جد letters — a dry echo on release.
أ إ ؤ ئ ء — all the same clean catch in the throat.
Squeezed and buzzing; you can hold it.
Same place as ع, no buzz.

slides.heading: The vowel is the tell
body: ص ض ط ظ are the heavy letters. Heavy does not mean loud — it means the back of your tongue lifts toward the roof of your mouth while the front does the work.
Here is the thing nobody tells beginners: you cannot really hear that dome on the consonant itself. You hear it on the VOWEL beside it.
After a heavy letter, a fatha backs toward the ‘o’ in ‘hot’ — صَ is closer to ‘ṣo’ than to ‘sa’. A damma goes deep and round. A kasra resists most, but still pulls back a little.
A long alif after a heavy letter is the clearest tell of all — a heavy alif, dark and resonant.
Your own diagnostic, and you can run it without me: say سَا, then صَا. If they sound the same, the dome is not happening yet.

audio.cue: ص: tip of the tongue at the lower front teeth — the same place as س — but with the back of the tongue domed. A thick, heavy whistle.

slides.makhraj: tip of the tongue against the lower front teeth, with the tongue-body raised
notes: Revision letter from Lesson 1.4 — today it lives inside words, which is much harder than saying it alone.
ص is simply س with the tongue-body lifted. Everything else — the place, the whistle, the lack of voice — is identical.
The heaviness must survive all the way to the END of the letter. It most often collapses at the moment you stop, which is why the sukūn words matter.

slides.heading: ص inside real words — start, middle, end
slides.instructions: Read right to left. Before each word, say the light twin out loud (سَا) and then the heavy one (صَا), so the tongue knows which shape to take.

audio.cue: Read صَبْر right to left: ṣaad + fatha (ṣa, heavy), ba with sukūn (b), ra (r), then blend: ṣabr — “patience”. The model word. The fatha is backed — closer to ‘ṣo’ than to the ‘a’ in ‘cat’.
Read صَدْر right to left: ṣaad + fatha (ṣa, heavy), dal with sukūn (d — it bounces), ra (r), then blend: ṣadr — “chest”. Same shape as صَبْر. Drill them as a pair.

Read صُبْح right to left: ṣaad + damma (ṣu, heavy and round), ba with sukūn (b), ḥaa (ḥ), then blend: ṣubḥ — “morning”. Heavy ص at the front, throat ح at the back — both of your hard letters in three sounds.
Read صَيْف right to left: ṣaad + fatha (ṣay, heavy), yaa with sukūn (y), fa (f), then blend: ṣayf — “summer”. Hold this one — سَيْف ‘sword’ is coming in the next drill.

Read صِدْق right to left: ṣaad + kasra (ṣi, heavy), dal with sukūn (d), qaaf (q), then blend: ṣidq — “truth”. Kasra is the hard vowel on a heavy letter — the ص must stay heavy even though the vowel is bright.
Read عَصْر right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), ṣaad with sukūn (ṣ, heavy), ra (r), then blend: ʿaṣr — “afternoon, time”. The ص makes the ر heavy too — that is the knock-on effect to listen for.
Read نَصْر right to left: nun + fatha (na), ṣaad with sukūn (ṣ, heavy), ra (r), then blend: naṣr — “help, victory”. A light ن first makes the switch to heavy audible.

Read بَصَر right to left: ba + fatha (ba, light), ṣaad + fatha (ṣa, heavy), ra (r), then blend: baṣar — “sight”. Two fathas: the first light, the second backed. The single best word for hearing what ص does to a vowel.
Read مِصْر right to left: meem + kasra (mi), ṣaad with sukūn (ṣ, heavy), ra (r), then blend: miṣr — “Egypt”.

Read فَصْل right to left: fa + fatha (fa), ṣaad with sukūn (ṣ, heavy), lam (l), then blend: faṣl — “separation, season”. Note the ل stays LIGHT after the ص. Only ر follows the heaviness across — ل does not.

Read قَمِيص right to left: qaaf + fatha (qa), meem + long ī (mī), ṣaad (ṣ, heavy), then blend: qamīṣ — “shirt”. The long ī is bright, then it must retract into the ص at the very last moment. Most students stay bright and miss it.
Read نَقْص right to left: nun + fatha (na), qaaf with sukūn (q — it bounces), ṣaad (ṣ), then blend: naqṣ — “loss, decrease”.

Read خَالِص right to left: khaa + long ā (khā, heavy), lam + kasra (li, light), ṣaad (ṣ, heavy), then blend: khāliṣ — “pure”. Heavy, then light, then heavy again. Turning the heaviness off and back on is harder than keeping it on.
Read حَرِيص right to left: ḥaa + fatha (ḥa), ra + long ī (rī), ṣaad (ṣ), then blend: ḥarīṣ — “eager, keen”.

Read قِصَاص right to left: qaaf + kasra (qi), ṣaad + long ā (ṣā, heavy), ṣaad (ṣ), then blend: qiṣāṣ — “retaliation”. Two ṣaads around a heavy alif — the longest stretch of heaviness in the lesson. Save it for last.

slides.heading: ص or س? — read down each column
slides.instructions: Same makhraj, same whistle. The ONLY difference is whether the back of the tongue is domed. Read each pair back to back.

audio.cue: Read صَيْف right to left: ṣaad + fatha (ṣay, heavy), yaa with sukūn, fa, then blend: ṣayf — “summer”.
Read سَيْف right to left: seen + fatha (say, light), yaa with sukūn, fa, then blend: sayf — “sword”. Same word, one feature apart: the tongue-body is flat for س and domed for ص.
Read نَصْر right to left: nun + fatha, ṣaad with sukūn (heavy), ra, then blend: naṣr — “help, victory”.
Read نَسْر right to left: nun + fatha, seen with sukūn (light), ra, then blend: nasr — “vulture”.
Read صَدَّ right to left: ṣaad + fatha (heavy), dal with a shadda (dd), then blend: ṣadda — “he turned away”.
Read سَدَّ right to left: seen + fatha (light), dal with a shadda (dd), then blend: sadda — “he blocked”.
ض: the SIDE of the tongue presses against the upper molars — either side works — with the tongue-body domed. The sound stretches along the edge of the tongue.

slides.makhraj: the side of the tongue against the upper molars
notes: Revision letter from Lesson 1.4, and the most mis-taught letter in Arabic.
ض is NOT د with extra weight. د is the tongue-TIP on the gum ridge; ض is the tongue-SIDE on the molars. Different place entirely.
Use ضِدّ as your self-test: it puts ض and د in one syllable. If they sound the same, the ض has collapsed into a heavy د.

slides.heading: ض inside real words — start, middle, end
slides.instructions: Read right to left. ض is made with the SIDE of the tongue against the upper molars — not the tip. Check ضِدّ first: if the ض and the د sound alike, stop and fix it before going on.

audio.cue: Read ضِدّ right to left: ḍaad + kasra (ḍi, heavy), dal with a shadda (dd), then blend: ḍidd — “opposite”. THE diagnostic word. ض then د in one syllable. If the two sound the same, the ض is wrong — start again.
Read ضُحَى right to left: ḍaad + damma (ḍu, heavy and deep), ḥaa + long ā (ḥā), then blend: ḍuḥā — “forenoon”. You know this sūrah. ض then ح — both far back in the mouth and throat.

Read ضَرَبَ right to left: ḍaad + fatha (ḍa, backed to ‘ḍo’), ra + fatha (ra), ba + fatha (ba), then blend: ḍaraba — “he struck”. The ر comes out heavy because the fatha before it is backed. Then everything lightens again.
Read ضَيْف right to left: ḍaad + fatha (ḍay, heavy), yaa with sukūn (y), fa (f), then blend: ḍayf — “guest”. Compare with صَيْف — same frame, a different heavy letter.
Read ضَعِيف right to left: ḍaad + fatha (ḍa, heavy), ʿayn + kasra (ʿi), long ī, fa (f), then blend: ḍaʿīf — “weak”. Molars, then deep throat — a real workout, and both are letters you are working on.
Read فَضْل right to left: fa + fatha (fa), ḍaad with sukūn (ḍ, heavy), lam (l), then blend: faḍl — “bounty, favour”. A sukūn means you must HOLD the molar contact, not flick past it.
Read غَضَب right to left: ghayn + fatha (gha), ḍaad + fatha (ḍa, heavy), ba (b), then blend: ghaḍab — “anger”.
Read قَضَى right to left: qaaf + fatha (qa), ḍaad + long ā (ḍā, heavy alif), then blend: qaḍā — “he decreed”.

Read رَضِيَ right to left: ra + fatha (ra), ḍaad + kasra (ḍi, still heavy), yaa + fatha (ya), then blend: raḍiya — “he was pleased”. Kasra on ض fights the natural pull backwards. Keep the molars engaged anyway.
Read خَضِر right to left: khaa + fatha (kha), ḍaad + kasra (ḍi, heavy), ra (r), then blend: khaḍir — “green”.
Read أَرْض right to left: hamza + fatha (a), ra with sukūn (r), ḍaad (ḍ, heavy), then blend: arḍ — “earth, land”. The most frequent ض word in the Qurʾān.
Read بَعْض right to left: ba + fatha (ba), ʿayn with sukūn (ʿ), ḍaad (ḍ, heavy), then blend: baʿḍ — “some”. Your two hard letters in one short word.
Read بَيْض right to left: ba + fatha (bay), yaa with sukūn (y), ḍaad (ḍ, heavy), then blend: bayḍ — “eggs”.
Read مَرِيض right to left: meem + fatha (ma), ra + long ī (rī), ḍaad (ḍ, heavy), then blend: marīḍ — “sick”. Same challenge as قَمِيص — the bright long ī has to retract into a heavy letter.
Read حَوْض right to left: ḥaa + fatha (ḥaw), waaw with sukūn (w), ḍaad (ḍ, heavy), then blend: ḥawḍ — “basin, pool”.

slides.heading: ض or د? — read down each column
slides.instructions: ض uses the side of the tongue on the molars; د uses the tip on the gum ridge. Different places, not just different weights.

audio.cue: Read ضَلَّ right to left: ḍaad + fatha (heavy), lam with a shadda (ll), then blend: ḍalla — “he went astray”. Side of the tongue against the upper molars.

Read دَلَّ right to left: dal + fatha (light), lam with a shadda (ll), then blend: dalla — “he showed the way”. Tip of the tongue on the gum ridge. Near-opposite meanings — mispronouncing this inverts the sense.
Read عَضَّ right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), ḍaad with a shadda (ḍḍ, heavy), then blend: ʿaḍḍa — “he bit”.
Read عَدَّ right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), dal with a shadda (dd, light), then blend: ʿadda — “he counted”.
Read ضَرْب right to left: ḍaad + fatha (heavy), ra with sukūn, ba, then blend: ḍarb — “striking”.
Read دَرْب right to left: dal + fatha (light), ra with sukūn, ba, then blend: darb — “path, road”.

slides.heading: ض and ظ, one āyah apart
body: In Sūrah al-Qiyāmah two consecutive āyāt read: وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ نَاضِرَة (75:22) — ‘faces that day are radiant’ — then إِلَىٰ رَبِّهَا نَاظِرَة (75:23) — ‘looking toward their Lord’.
One letter apart. Both heavy. Both correct in their own place, and each is wrong in the other’s.
This is the clearest proof in the whole Qurʾān that ض and ظ are different letters and not two spellings of one sound.
The difference is not weight — both are heavy. It is WHERE the tongue is: ض on the molars with the tip down, ظ with the tip out between the teeth.

slides.heading: ض or ظ? — read down each column
slides.instructions: Both are heavy, so weight will not tell them apart. Watch the tongue TIP: if you can see it between the teeth it is ظ; if it stays down it is ض.

audio.cue: Read ضَلَّ right to left: ḍaad — SIDE of the tongue on the molars, tip stays down, then blend: ḍalla — “he went astray”.
Read ظَلَّ right to left: ẓhaa — TIP of the tongue between the teeth, then blend: ẓalla — “he remained, became”. Both are heavy. The difference is not weight, it is WHERE the tongue is.
Read نَاضِرَة right to left: nun + long ā, ḍaad + kasra (heavy, molars), ra + fatha, taa marbūṭa, then blend: nāḍirah — “radiant, glowing”.

Read نَاظِرَة right to left: nun + long ā, ẓhaa + kasra (heavy, tongue-tip between teeth), ra + fatha, taa marbūṭa, then blend: nāẓirah — “looking, gazing”. These two sit one āyah apart in Sūrah al-Qiyāmah (75:22–23). One letter, two meanings, side by side.
Read حَضّ right to left: ḥaa + fatha (ḥa), ḍaad with a shadda (ḍḍ), then blend: ḥaḍḍ — “urging”.
Read حَظّ right to left: ḥaa + fatha (ḥa), ẓhaa with a shadda (ẓẓ), then blend: ḥaẓẓ — “share, portion”. Doubled letters hold the contrast open twice as long — nowhere to hide.
ط: same place as ت — the tongue-tip on the gum ridge — but with a full, domed mouth cavity. Heavy, and it bounces when it carries a sukūn.

slides.makhraj: tip of the tongue against the upper gum ridge, with the tongue-body raised
notes: Revision letter from Lesson 1.4. ط is the heavy twin of ت, at exactly the same place.
ط is also one of the five qalqalah letters (ق ط ب ج د), so a ط with a sukūn must bounce — and it is the only letter that is both heavy AND bouncing.
The hardest case is ط with a kasra (بَاطِل, طِين): the consonant must stay heavy even though the vowel is bright.

slides.heading: ط inside real words — start, middle, end
slides.instructions: Read right to left. Every ط is heavy in every vowel. Where a ط carries a sukūn it also bounces — those are marked in the cue.

audio.cue: Read طِين right to left: ṭaa + kasra (ṭi, heavy), long ī, nun (n), then blend: ṭīn — “clay”. The kasra test-case. Tongue broad and flat on the gum ridge, back of the tongue raised, THEN the ‘ee’.
Read طَيْر right to left: ṭaa + fatha (ṭay, heavy), yaa with sukūn (y), ra (r), then blend: ṭayr — “bird”. Fully backed: ‘ṭoyr’, not ‘tayr’.
Read طُور right to left: ṭaa + damma (ṭu, heavy), long ū, ra (r), then blend: ṭūr — “mount”. The easiest one here — the damma already pulls your mouth where ط wants it.

Read طَعَام right to left: ṭaa + fatha (ṭa, heavy), ʿayn + long ā (ʿā), meem (m), then blend: ṭaʿām — “food”. Heavy ط, then the throat opens for ع. A good transition drill for two of your hard letters.
Read طِفْل right to left: ṭaa + kasra (ṭi, heavy), fa with sukūn (f), lam (l), then blend: ṭifl — “child”. Careful: the sukūn is on the ف, not the ط — so there is no bounce here.
Read مَطَر right to left: meem + fatha (ma, light), ṭaa + fatha (ṭa, heavy), ra (r), then blend: maṭar — “rain”. The best word for hearing you switch weight mid-word.
Read بَطْن right to left: ba + fatha (ba), ṭaa with SUKŪN (ṭ — it bounces), nun (n), then blend: baṭn — “belly”. Qalqalah: ‘baṭ-eh-n’. The bounce lands before the ن.

Read نُطْفَة right to left: nun + damma (nu), ṭaa with SUKŪN (ṭ — bounce), fa + fatha (fa), taa marbūṭa, then blend: nuṭfah — “a drop”. The bounce must be audible before the whispered ف, or it disappears completely.

Read بَاطِل right to left: ba + long ā (bā), ṭaa + kasra (ṭi, still heavy), lam (l), then blend: bāṭil — “falsehood”. ط with a kasra mid-word — the classic failure point. Heavy consonant, bright vowel.
Read شَيْطَان right to left: sheen + fatha (shay), yaa with sukūn, ṭaa + long ā (ṭā, heavy), nun, then blend: shayṭān — “devil”. The most frequent ط word in the Qurʾān — worth over-drilling.

Read صِرَاط right to left: ṣaad + kasra (ṣi, heavy), ra + long ā (rā), ṭaa (ṭ, heavy), then blend: ṣirāṭ — “path”. You recite this every day in al-Fātiḥah. Two heavy letters bracket the word; stopping on it gives ‘ṣirāṭ-eh’.
Read لُوط right to left: lam + damma and long ū (lū), ṭaa (ṭ, heavy), then blend: lūṭ — “Lot (prophet)”. The simplest possible final-ط bounce.
Read خَيْط right to left: khaa + fatha (khay), yaa with sukūn (y), ṭaa (ṭ), then blend: khayṭ — “thread”.

Read قِسْط right to left: qaaf + kasra (qi), seen with sukūn (s, LIGHT), ṭaa (ṭ, HEAVY), then blend: qisṭ — “justice”. A light س immediately followed by a heavy ط — a hard junction, and a valuable one.
Read مُحِيط right to left: meem + damma (mu), ḥaa + long ī (ḥī), ṭaa (ṭ, heavy), then blend: muḥīṭ — “encompassing”. ح and ط in one short word — two of your five hard letters.

slides.heading: ط or ت? — read down each column
slides.instructions: The heavy twin and the light twin, same makhraj. Listen to the VOWEL, not the consonant — it is the vowel that gives it away.

audio.cue: Read طِين right to left: ṭaa + kasra (heavy), long ī, nun, then blend: ṭīn — “clay”.
Read تِين right to left: ta + kasra (light), long ī, nun, then blend: tīn — “fig”. The canonical pair, and both are Qurʾānic. Start every ط session here.
Read طَابَ right to left: ṭaa + long ā (heavy alif), ba + fatha, then blend: ṭāba — “it was good”.
Read تَابَ right to left: ta + long ā (light alif), ba + fatha, then blend: tāba — “he repented”.
Read طَمَّ right to left: ṭaa + fatha (heavy), meem with a shadda, then blend: ṭamma — “it overwhelmed”.
Read تَمَّ right to left: ta + fatha (light), meem with a shadda, then blend: tamma — “it was completed”. The shortest pair — good for rapid-fire alternation.
ظ: tongue-tip between the teeth — the same place as ذ and ث — voiced, and with the tongue-body domed. Heavy, and never bounced.

slides.makhraj: tip of the tongue between the front teeth, with the tongue-body raised
notes: Revision letter from Lesson 1.4. ظ is the heavy twin of ذ, at exactly the same place.
The commonest error is not saying ذ — it is saying ز, or a heavy د. Both keep the tongue-tip hidden. If you cannot see the tip, it is wrong.
ظ is NOT a qalqalah letter. On a sukūn it is held and allowed to fade — never bounced. That is the contrast with ط.

slides.heading: ظ inside real words
slides.instructions: ظ is the heavy twin of ذ: tongue-tip BETWEEN the teeth, voiced, heavy. If you cannot see the tip, it is not ظ.

audio.cue: Read ظُلْم right to left: ẓhaa + damma (ẓu, heavy), lam with sukūn (l), meem (m), then blend: ẓulm — “injustice”. The sukūn is on the ل, not the ظ.
Read ظِلّ right to left: ẓhaa + kasra (ẓi, still heavy), lam with a shadda (ll), then blend: ẓill — “shade”. Kasra on ظ — the tongue-tip must still show between the teeth.
Read ظَنَّ right to left: ẓhaa + fatha (ẓa, heavy), nun with a shadda (nn), then blend: ẓanna — “he thought”. The shortest ظ word there is. Ideal first drill.
Read ظَهْر right to left: ẓhaa + fatha (ẓa, heavy), haa with sukūn (h), ra (r), then blend: ẓahr — “back”. ظ then ه — two completely different breath sources back to back.

Read عَظِيم right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), ẓhaa + kasra (ẓi, heavy), long ī, meem (m), then blend: ʿaẓīm — “great”. Very high frequency, and it uses the hardest vowel on ظ. You will meet it constantly.
Read نَظَرَ right to left: nun + fatha (na, light), ẓhaa + fatha (ẓa, heavy), ra + fatha (ra), then blend: naẓara — “he looked”. Light, heavy, light — the switch has to happen twice.

Read عَظْم right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), ẓhaa with SUKŪN (ẓ — HOLD it, do not bounce), meem (m), then blend: ʿaẓm — “bone”. The best word in the lesson for the ط/ظ contrast: press the tongue-tip between the teeth and sustain, then release into the م.
Read حَظّ right to left: ḥaa + fatha (ḥa), ẓhaa with a shadda (ẓẓ), then blend: ḥaẓẓ — “share, portion”.
Read حَافِظ right to left: ḥaa + long ā (ḥā), fa + kasra (fi), ẓhaa (ẓ, heavy), then blend: ḥāfiẓ — “guardian”.
Read غَيْظ right to left: ghayn + fatha (ghay), yaa with sukūn (y), ẓhaa (ẓ, heavy), then blend: ghayẓ — “rage”. غ and ظ are both deep — the whole word sits low and back.

slides.heading: ظ or ذ or ز? — read down each column
slides.instructions: ذ is the same place but light. ز is a whistle from behind the teeth. Only ظ is both between-the-teeth and heavy.

audio.cue: Read نَظَرَ right to left: ẓhaa — heavy, tongue-tip between the teeth, then blend: naẓara — “he looked”.
Read نَذَرَ right to left: dhal — LIGHT, same tongue-tip position, then blend: nadhara — “he vowed”. Same place, the only difference is weight. The best ظ/ذ pair there is.
Read ظَهْر right to left: ẓhaa — tongue-tip between the teeth, then blend: ẓahr — “back”.
Read زَهْر right to left: zay — tongue BEHIND the teeth, a sharp whistle, then blend: zahr — “blossom”. This is the substitution you are most likely to make. If it whistles, it became ز.
Read عَظْم right to left: ẓhaa with sukūn — held, then blend: ʿaẓm — “bone”.
Read عَزْم right to left: zay with sukūn — whistled, then blend: ʿazm — “resolve”. Both Qurʾānic, both with a sukūn — a perfectly matched pair.

slides.heading: Bounce or hold? — ط against ظ
slides.instructions: ط is a qalqalah letter and bounces on a sukūn. ظ is NOT and must be held. Read across, twice.

audio.cue: Read بَطْن right to left: ṭaa with sukūn — BOUNCE, ‘baṭ-eh-n’, then blend: baṭn — “belly”.
Read عَظْم right to left: ẓhaa with sukūn — HOLD, no echo, then blend: ʿaẓm — “bone”.
Read قُطْن right to left: ṭaa with sukūn — BOUNCE, ‘quṭ-eh-n’, then blend: quṭn — “cotton”.
Read عَزْم right to left: zay with sukūn — no bounce, and no ظ either, then blend: ʿazm — “resolve”. Run the four across, in order, twice. ط bounces; ظ never does.

slides.heading: وَلَا الضَّالِّينَ — the ض you say seventeen times a day
body: The last words of al-Fātiḥah: وَلَا ٱلضَّآلِّينَ — ‘and not of those who go astray’. You say this in every rakʿah, so any error here sets hard.
One — do not say ظ. ٱلظَّالِّينَ is a different word from a different root, meaning ‘those who persist’. Keep the tongue-tip DOWN and away from the teeth; all the work is at the molars.
Two — do not say د. Dropping the dome turns it into ‘ad-dāllīn’.
Three — the madd is long. The alif here is followed by a doubled lām, which makes it a six-count lengthening: the longest in tajwīd. It should feel uncomfortably long. Beginners give it two.
Four — hold the shadda. The ل of الـ has assimilated into the ض, which is why it is doubled: al- + ḍāllīn becomes aḍ-ḍāllīn. Two full counts of molar contact.
Five — keep the alif heavy. After a ض the long ‘aa’ must stay dark and backed. A bright ‘aa’ undoes a correct ض.

slides.heading: Hear a reciter — ص and ض in the Qurʾān
slides.instructions: The exact words as they appear in the Qurʾān. Tap to hear a qāriʾ, then copy him. Listen for how the vowel darkens after the heavy letter.

slides.heading: Hear a reciter — ط and ظ in the Qurʾān
slides.instructions: Tap and copy. On نُّطْفَةٍ and ٱلْعَظْمُ especially: one of those bounces and one is held.

audio.cue: Same place as س, tongue-body domed. Test: سَا then صَا.
Not a heavy د. The SIDE of the tongue on the upper molars. Test: ضِدّ.

items.name: ṭaa — heavy ت, and it bounces

audio.cue: Same place as ت, domed. On a sukūn it bounces. Test: طِين then تِين.

items.name: ẓhaa — heavy ذ, and it is held

audio.cue: Tongue-tip between the teeth, voiced and heavy. On a sukūn it is HELD, never bounced.

slides.heading: Homework — 15–20 min/day
tasks: Warm up every session with سَا / صَا and تَا / طَا, three times each, before reading anything
Read the ص word set and the ض word set aloud daily — all three rows of each
Check ضِدّ every single day: if the ض and the د sound alike, do nothing else until they do not
Read the ط word set daily, bouncing every ط that carries a sukūn (بَطْن, نُطْفَة)
Read the ظ word set daily, holding every ظ — never bouncing it
Bounce-or-hold drill across: بَطْن — عَظْم — قُطْن — عَزْم, twice through
Read the four minimal-pair sets ACROSS the page, not down: ص/س, ض/د, ض/ظ, ط/ت
Tap through both reciter rows once a day and copy the qāriʾ aloud
Say وَلَا ٱلضَّآلِّينَ slowly once a day, counting the madd to six

drills.title: ص inside real words — start, middle, end
drills.instructions: Read right to left. Before each word, say the light twin out loud (سَا) and then the heavy one (صَا), so the tongue knows which shape to take.

audio.cue: Read صَبْر right to left: ṣaad + fatha (ṣa, heavy), ba with sukūn (b), ra (r), then blend: ṣabr — “patience”. The model word. The fatha is backed — closer to ‘ṣo’ than to the ‘a’ in ‘cat’.
Read صَدْر right to left: ṣaad + fatha (ṣa, heavy), dal with sukūn (d — it bounces), ra (r), then blend: ṣadr — “chest”. Same shape as صَبْر. Drill them as a pair.

Read صُبْح right to left: ṣaad + damma (ṣu, heavy and round), ba with sukūn (b), ḥaa (ḥ), then blend: ṣubḥ — “morning”. Heavy ص at the front, throat ح at the back — both of your hard letters in three sounds.
Read صَيْف right to left: ṣaad + fatha (ṣay, heavy), yaa with sukūn (y), fa (f), then blend: ṣayf — “summer”. Hold this one — سَيْف ‘sword’ is coming in the next drill.

Read صِدْق right to left: ṣaad + kasra (ṣi, heavy), dal with sukūn (d), qaaf (q), then blend: ṣidq — “truth”. Kasra is the hard vowel on a heavy letter — the ص must stay heavy even though the vowel is bright.
Read عَصْر right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), ṣaad with sukūn (ṣ, heavy), ra (r), then blend: ʿaṣr — “afternoon, time”. The ص makes the ر heavy too — that is the knock-on effect to listen for.
Read نَصْر right to left: nun + fatha (na), ṣaad with sukūn (ṣ, heavy), ra (r), then blend: naṣr — “help, victory”. A light ن first makes the switch to heavy audible.

Read بَصَر right to left: ba + fatha (ba, light), ṣaad + fatha (ṣa, heavy), ra (r), then blend: baṣar — “sight”. Two fathas: the first light, the second backed. The single best word for hearing what ص does to a vowel.
Read مِصْر right to left: meem + kasra (mi), ṣaad with sukūn (ṣ, heavy), ra (r), then blend: miṣr — “Egypt”.

Read فَصْل right to left: fa + fatha (fa), ṣaad with sukūn (ṣ, heavy), lam (l), then blend: faṣl — “separation, season”. Note the ل stays LIGHT after the ص. Only ر follows the heaviness across — ل does not.

Read قَمِيص right to left: qaaf + fatha (qa), meem + long ī (mī), ṣaad (ṣ, heavy), then blend: qamīṣ — “shirt”. The long ī is bright, then it must retract into the ص at the very last moment. Most students stay bright and miss it.
Read نَقْص right to left: nun + fatha (na), qaaf with sukūn (q — it bounces), ṣaad (ṣ), then blend: naqṣ — “loss, decrease”.

Read خَالِص right to left: khaa + long ā (khā, heavy), lam + kasra (li, light), ṣaad (ṣ, heavy), then blend: khāliṣ — “pure”. Heavy, then light, then heavy again. Turning the heaviness off and back on is harder than keeping it on.
Read حَرِيص right to left: ḥaa + fatha (ḥa), ra + long ī (rī), ṣaad (ṣ), then blend: ḥarīṣ — “eager, keen”.

Read قِصَاص right to left: qaaf + kasra (qi), ṣaad + long ā (ṣā, heavy), ṣaad (ṣ), then blend: qiṣāṣ — “retaliation”. Two ṣaads around a heavy alif — the longest stretch of heaviness in the lesson. Save it for last.

drills.title: ص or س? — read down each column
drills.instructions: Same makhraj, same whistle. The ONLY difference is whether the back of the tongue is domed. Read each pair back to back.

audio.cue: Read صَيْف right to left: ṣaad + fatha (ṣay, heavy), yaa with sukūn, fa, then blend: ṣayf — “summer”.
Read سَيْف right to left: seen + fatha (say, light), yaa with sukūn, fa, then blend: sayf — “sword”. Same word, one feature apart: the tongue-body is flat for س and domed for ص.
Read نَصْر right to left: nun + fatha, ṣaad with sukūn (heavy), ra, then blend: naṣr — “help, victory”.
Read نَسْر right to left: nun + fatha, seen with sukūn (light), ra, then blend: nasr — “vulture”.
Read صَدَّ right to left: ṣaad + fatha (heavy), dal with a shadda (dd), then blend: ṣadda — “he turned away”.
Read سَدَّ right to left: seen + fatha (light), dal with a shadda (dd), then blend: sadda — “he blocked”.

drills.title: ض inside real words — start, middle, end
drills.instructions: Read right to left. ض is made with the SIDE of the tongue against the upper molars — not the tip. Check ضِدّ first: if the ض and the د sound alike, stop and fix it before going on.

audio.cue: Read ضِدّ right to left: ḍaad + kasra (ḍi, heavy), dal with a shadda (dd), then blend: ḍidd — “opposite”. THE diagnostic word. ض then د in one syllable. If the two sound the same, the ض is wrong — start again.
Read ضُحَى right to left: ḍaad + damma (ḍu, heavy and deep), ḥaa + long ā (ḥā), then blend: ḍuḥā — “forenoon”. You know this sūrah. ض then ح — both far back in the mouth and throat.

Read ضَرَبَ right to left: ḍaad + fatha (ḍa, backed to ‘ḍo’), ra + fatha (ra), ba + fatha (ba), then blend: ḍaraba — “he struck”. The ر comes out heavy because the fatha before it is backed. Then everything lightens again.
Read ضَيْف right to left: ḍaad + fatha (ḍay, heavy), yaa with sukūn (y), fa (f), then blend: ḍayf — “guest”. Compare with صَيْف — same frame, a different heavy letter.
Read ضَعِيف right to left: ḍaad + fatha (ḍa, heavy), ʿayn + kasra (ʿi), long ī, fa (f), then blend: ḍaʿīf — “weak”. Molars, then deep throat — a real workout, and both are letters you are working on.
Read فَضْل right to left: fa + fatha (fa), ḍaad with sukūn (ḍ, heavy), lam (l), then blend: faḍl — “bounty, favour”. A sukūn means you must HOLD the molar contact, not flick past it.
Read غَضَب right to left: ghayn + fatha (gha), ḍaad + fatha (ḍa, heavy), ba (b), then blend: ghaḍab — “anger”.
Read قَضَى right to left: qaaf + fatha (qa), ḍaad + long ā (ḍā, heavy alif), then blend: qaḍā — “he decreed”.

Read رَضِيَ right to left: ra + fatha (ra), ḍaad + kasra (ḍi, still heavy), yaa + fatha (ya), then blend: raḍiya — “he was pleased”. Kasra on ض fights the natural pull backwards. Keep the molars engaged anyway.
Read خَضِر right to left: khaa + fatha (kha), ḍaad + kasra (ḍi, heavy), ra (r), then blend: khaḍir — “green”.
Read أَرْض right to left: hamza + fatha (a), ra with sukūn (r), ḍaad (ḍ, heavy), then blend: arḍ — “earth, land”. The most frequent ض word in the Qurʾān.
Read بَعْض right to left: ba + fatha (ba), ʿayn with sukūn (ʿ), ḍaad (ḍ, heavy), then blend: baʿḍ — “some”. Your two hard letters in one short word.
Read بَيْض right to left: ba + fatha (bay), yaa with sukūn (y), ḍaad (ḍ, heavy), then blend: bayḍ — “eggs”.
Read مَرِيض right to left: meem + fatha (ma), ra + long ī (rī), ḍaad (ḍ, heavy), then blend: marīḍ — “sick”. Same challenge as قَمِيص — the bright long ī has to retract into a heavy letter.
Read حَوْض right to left: ḥaa + fatha (ḥaw), waaw with sukūn (w), ḍaad (ḍ, heavy), then blend: ḥawḍ — “basin, pool”.

drills.title: ض or د? — read down each column
drills.instructions: ض uses the side of the tongue on the molars; د uses the tip on the gum ridge. Different places, not just different weights.

audio.cue: Read ضَلَّ right to left: ḍaad + fatha (heavy), lam with a shadda (ll), then blend: ḍalla — “he went astray”. Side of the tongue against the upper molars.

Read دَلَّ right to left: dal + fatha (light), lam with a shadda (ll), then blend: dalla — “he showed the way”. Tip of the tongue on the gum ridge. Near-opposite meanings — mispronouncing this inverts the sense.
Read عَضَّ right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), ḍaad with a shadda (ḍḍ, heavy), then blend: ʿaḍḍa — “he bit”.
Read عَدَّ right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), dal with a shadda (dd, light), then blend: ʿadda — “he counted”.
Read ضَرْب right to left: ḍaad + fatha (heavy), ra with sukūn, ba, then blend: ḍarb — “striking”.
Read دَرْب right to left: dal + fatha (light), ra with sukūn, ba, then blend: darb — “path, road”.

drills.title: ض or ظ? — read down each column
drills.instructions: Both are heavy, so weight will not tell them apart. Watch the tongue TIP: if you can see it between the teeth it is ظ; if it stays down it is ض.

audio.cue: Read ضَلَّ right to left: ḍaad — SIDE of the tongue on the molars, tip stays down, then blend: ḍalla — “he went astray”.
Read ظَلَّ right to left: ẓhaa — TIP of the tongue between the teeth, then blend: ẓalla — “he remained, became”. Both are heavy. The difference is not weight, it is WHERE the tongue is.
Read نَاضِرَة right to left: nun + long ā, ḍaad + kasra (heavy, molars), ra + fatha, taa marbūṭa, then blend: nāḍirah — “radiant, glowing”.

Read نَاظِرَة right to left: nun + long ā, ẓhaa + kasra (heavy, tongue-tip between teeth), ra + fatha, taa marbūṭa, then blend: nāẓirah — “looking, gazing”. These two sit one āyah apart in Sūrah al-Qiyāmah (75:22–23). One letter, two meanings, side by side.
Read حَضّ right to left: ḥaa + fatha (ḥa), ḍaad with a shadda (ḍḍ), then blend: ḥaḍḍ — “urging”.
Read حَظّ right to left: ḥaa + fatha (ḥa), ẓhaa with a shadda (ẓẓ), then blend: ḥaẓẓ — “share, portion”. Doubled letters hold the contrast open twice as long — nowhere to hide.

drills.title: ط inside real words — start, middle, end
drills.instructions: Read right to left. Every ط is heavy in every vowel. Where a ط carries a sukūn it also bounces — those are marked in the cue.

audio.cue: Read طِين right to left: ṭaa + kasra (ṭi, heavy), long ī, nun (n), then blend: ṭīn — “clay”. The kasra test-case. Tongue broad and flat on the gum ridge, back of the tongue raised, THEN the ‘ee’.
Read طَيْر right to left: ṭaa + fatha (ṭay, heavy), yaa with sukūn (y), ra (r), then blend: ṭayr — “bird”. Fully backed: ‘ṭoyr’, not ‘tayr’.
Read طُور right to left: ṭaa + damma (ṭu, heavy), long ū, ra (r), then blend: ṭūr — “mount”. The easiest one here — the damma already pulls your mouth where ط wants it.

Read طَعَام right to left: ṭaa + fatha (ṭa, heavy), ʿayn + long ā (ʿā), meem (m), then blend: ṭaʿām — “food”. Heavy ط, then the throat opens for ع. A good transition drill for two of your hard letters.
Read طِفْل right to left: ṭaa + kasra (ṭi, heavy), fa with sukūn (f), lam (l), then blend: ṭifl — “child”. Careful: the sukūn is on the ف, not the ط — so there is no bounce here.
Read مَطَر right to left: meem + fatha (ma, light), ṭaa + fatha (ṭa, heavy), ra (r), then blend: maṭar — “rain”. The best word for hearing you switch weight mid-word.
Read بَطْن right to left: ba + fatha (ba), ṭaa with SUKŪN (ṭ — it bounces), nun (n), then blend: baṭn — “belly”. Qalqalah: ‘baṭ-eh-n’. The bounce lands before the ن.

Read نُطْفَة right to left: nun + damma (nu), ṭaa with SUKŪN (ṭ — bounce), fa + fatha (fa), taa marbūṭa, then blend: nuṭfah — “a drop”. The bounce must be audible before the whispered ف, or it disappears completely.

Read بَاطِل right to left: ba + long ā (bā), ṭaa + kasra (ṭi, still heavy), lam (l), then blend: bāṭil — “falsehood”. ط with a kasra mid-word — the classic failure point. Heavy consonant, bright vowel.
Read شَيْطَان right to left: sheen + fatha (shay), yaa with sukūn, ṭaa + long ā (ṭā, heavy), nun, then blend: shayṭān — “devil”. The most frequent ط word in the Qurʾān — worth over-drilling.

Read صِرَاط right to left: ṣaad + kasra (ṣi, heavy), ra + long ā (rā), ṭaa (ṭ, heavy), then blend: ṣirāṭ — “path”. You recite this every day in al-Fātiḥah. Two heavy letters bracket the word; stopping on it gives ‘ṣirāṭ-eh’.
Read لُوط right to left: lam + damma and long ū (lū), ṭaa (ṭ, heavy), then blend: lūṭ — “Lot (prophet)”. The simplest possible final-ط bounce.
Read خَيْط right to left: khaa + fatha (khay), yaa with sukūn (y), ṭaa (ṭ), then blend: khayṭ — “thread”.

Read قِسْط right to left: qaaf + kasra (qi), seen with sukūn (s, LIGHT), ṭaa (ṭ, HEAVY), then blend: qisṭ — “justice”. A light س immediately followed by a heavy ط — a hard junction, and a valuable one.
Read مُحِيط right to left: meem + damma (mu), ḥaa + long ī (ḥī), ṭaa (ṭ, heavy), then blend: muḥīṭ — “encompassing”. ح and ط in one short word — two of your five hard letters.

drills.title: ط or ت? — read down each column
drills.instructions: The heavy twin and the light twin, same makhraj. Listen to the VOWEL, not the consonant — it is the vowel that gives it away.

audio.cue: Read طِين right to left: ṭaa + kasra (heavy), long ī, nun, then blend: ṭīn — “clay”.
Read تِين right to left: ta + kasra (light), long ī, nun, then blend: tīn — “fig”. The canonical pair, and both are Qurʾānic. Start every ط session here.
Read طَابَ right to left: ṭaa + long ā (heavy alif), ba + fatha, then blend: ṭāba — “it was good”.
Read تَابَ right to left: ta + long ā (light alif), ba + fatha, then blend: tāba — “he repented”.
Read طَمَّ right to left: ṭaa + fatha (heavy), meem with a shadda, then blend: ṭamma — “it overwhelmed”.
Read تَمَّ right to left: ta + fatha (light), meem with a shadda, then blend: tamma — “it was completed”. The shortest pair — good for rapid-fire alternation.

drills.title: ظ inside real words
drills.instructions: ظ is the heavy twin of ذ: tongue-tip BETWEEN the teeth, voiced, heavy. If you cannot see the tip, it is not ظ.

audio.cue: Read ظُلْم right to left: ẓhaa + damma (ẓu, heavy), lam with sukūn (l), meem (m), then blend: ẓulm — “injustice”. The sukūn is on the ل, not the ظ.
Read ظِلّ right to left: ẓhaa + kasra (ẓi, still heavy), lam with a shadda (ll), then blend: ẓill — “shade”. Kasra on ظ — the tongue-tip must still show between the teeth.
Read ظَنَّ right to left: ẓhaa + fatha (ẓa, heavy), nun with a shadda (nn), then blend: ẓanna — “he thought”. The shortest ظ word there is. Ideal first drill.
Read ظَهْر right to left: ẓhaa + fatha (ẓa, heavy), haa with sukūn (h), ra (r), then blend: ẓahr — “back”. ظ then ه — two completely different breath sources back to back.

Read عَظِيم right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), ẓhaa + kasra (ẓi, heavy), long ī, meem (m), then blend: ʿaẓīm — “great”. Very high frequency, and it uses the hardest vowel on ظ. You will meet it constantly.
Read نَظَرَ right to left: nun + fatha (na, light), ẓhaa + fatha (ẓa, heavy), ra + fatha (ra), then blend: naẓara — “he looked”. Light, heavy, light — the switch has to happen twice.

Read عَظْم right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), ẓhaa with SUKŪN (ẓ — HOLD it, do not bounce), meem (m), then blend: ʿaẓm — “bone”. The best word in the lesson for the ط/ظ contrast: press the tongue-tip between the teeth and sustain, then release into the م.
Read حَظّ right to left: ḥaa + fatha (ḥa), ẓhaa with a shadda (ẓẓ), then blend: ḥaẓẓ — “share, portion”.
Read حَافِظ right to left: ḥaa + long ā (ḥā), fa + kasra (fi), ẓhaa (ẓ, heavy), then blend: ḥāfiẓ — “guardian”.
Read غَيْظ right to left: ghayn + fatha (ghay), yaa with sukūn (y), ẓhaa (ẓ, heavy), then blend: ghayẓ — “rage”. غ and ظ are both deep — the whole word sits low and back.

drills.title: ظ or ذ or ز? — read down each column
drills.instructions: ذ is the same place but light. ز is a whistle from behind the teeth. Only ظ is both between-the-teeth and heavy.

audio.cue: Read نَظَرَ right to left: ẓhaa — heavy, tongue-tip between the teeth, then blend: naẓara — “he looked”.
Read نَذَرَ right to left: dhal — LIGHT, same tongue-tip position, then blend: nadhara — “he vowed”. Same place, the only difference is weight. The best ظ/ذ pair there is.
Read ظَهْر right to left: ẓhaa — tongue-tip between the teeth, then blend: ẓahr — “back”.
Read زَهْر right to left: zay — tongue BEHIND the teeth, a sharp whistle, then blend: zahr — “blossom”. This is the substitution you are most likely to make. If it whistles, it became ز.
Read عَظْم right to left: ẓhaa with sukūn — held, then blend: ʿaẓm — “bone”.
Read عَزْم right to left: zay with sukūn — whistled, then blend: ʿazm — “resolve”. Both Qurʾānic, both with a sukūn — a perfectly matched pair.

drills.title: Bounce or hold? — ط against ظ
drills.instructions: ط is a qalqalah letter and bounces on a sukūn. ظ is NOT and must be held. Read across, twice.

audio.cue: Read بَطْن right to left: ṭaa with sukūn — BOUNCE, ‘baṭ-eh-n’, then blend: baṭn — “belly”.
Read عَظْم right to left: ẓhaa with sukūn — HOLD, no echo, then blend: ʿaẓm — “bone”.
Read قُطْن right to left: ṭaa with sukūn — BOUNCE, ‘quṭ-eh-n’, then blend: quṭn — “cotton”.
Read عَزْم right to left: zay with sukūn — no bounce, and no ظ either, then blend: ʿazm — “resolve”. Run the four across, in order, twice. ط bounces; ظ never does.

drills.title: Hear a reciter — ص and ض in the Qurʾān
drills.instructions: The exact words as they appear in the Qurʾān. Tap to hear a qāriʾ, then copy him. Listen for how the vowel darkens after the heavy letter.

drills.title: Hear a reciter — ط and ظ in the Qurʾān
drills.instructions: Tap and copy. On نُّطْفَةٍ and ٱلْعَظْمُ especially: one of those bounces and one is held.

dailyChecklist: Warm-up: سَا / صَا and تَا / طَا, three times each
ص word set and ض word set, all rows, read aloud
ضِدّ self-test — ض and د must not sound alike
ط word set, bouncing every ط that carries a sukūn
ظ word set, holding every ظ
Bounce-or-hold across: بَطْن — عَظْم — قُطْن — عَزْم, twice
The four minimal-pair sets read ACROSS: ص/س, ض/د, ض/ظ, ط/ت
Both reciter rows tapped and copied aloud
وَلَا ٱلضَّآلِّينَ once, with the madd counted to six

script: Open with the vowel, not the consonant. Say سَا then صَا back to back and ask her which sound moved — she will say the ‘a’. That is the whole lesson in ten seconds, and it hands her a self-test she can run at home.
Teach ص first. It is the easiest heavy letter because س is already solid, so it isolates one single change: the tongue-body dome.

For ض, spend the time on PLACE before weight. Say plainly that ض is not a heavy د — د is the tongue-tip on the gum ridge, ض is the tongue-side on the molars. Have her feel the contact with a finger against her cheek if that helps.
ضِدّ is the diagnostic. Do not move past ض while ضِدّ comes out with two identical sounds. It is worth stalling the lesson here.

Show her 75:22–23 side by side on the page. نَاضِرَة then نَاظِرَة, one āyah apart. Nothing you can say convinces a student that ض and ظ are genuinely different letters as fast as seeing the Qurʾān use both in consecutive lines.

Note on ض for you, not for her: the early grammarians describe a lateral sound that no living reciter produces. Teach the modern standard — a pharyngealised stop kept distinct from د and ظ. Do not chase the reconstructed classical ض; it will confuse her and no recitation tradition uses it.
For ط, join it back to last lesson: it is the only letter that is both heavy and bouncing. بَطْن and نُطْفَة are where both facts have to be true at once.
Then immediately contrast ظ. عَظْم against بَطْن is the single most useful drill on the page — same shape of word, one bounces and one does not.
Save al-Fātiḥah for the end, once ض is actually working. Correcting ٱلضَّآلِّينَ before the letter is secure just adds anxiety to something she recites seventeen times a day.
Run every minimal-pair set ACROSS, never down. Reading down a column lets her set the tongue once and coast; reading across forces a switch on every item.
Finish on the reciter clips. Hearing a qāriʾ darken the vowel after ص and ط is worth more than another explanation from you.
listenFor: Heaviness present on the consonant but absent from the vowel — she produces a recognisable ص and then a bright, front ‘a’ after it. This is the commonest partial success and it is easy to mistake for a pass.
Tafkhīm collapsing at the moment the letter stops, especially on a sukūn (فَضْل, عَصْر). Attention goes to the stop and the dome drops.
ض produced as a heavy د — tongue-tip on the gum ridge instead of the side on the molars. Check with ضِدّ, not with a word where ض stands alone.
ض produced as ظ, or ظ as ض. Watch the tongue-tip: visible between the teeth means ظ, hidden means ض. This is a place error, so weight cues will not catch it.
ظ collapsing to ز — the tip retreats behind the teeth and the sound whistles. The single most likely ظ error, more likely than ذ.
ظ bounced like ط. ظ is not a qalqalah letter; a bounce means she has swapped in a heavy د.
ط going light under a kasra (بَاطِل, طِين) even when it was heavy under a fatha. Heavy consonant plus bright vowel is the hardest combination in the lesson.
The ر after a heavy letter failing to go heavy (عَصْر, ضَرَبَ) — a knock-on effect she will not notice unless you name it.
In ٱلضَّآلِّينَ specifically: a short madd (two counts instead of six) — mangled more often than the ض itself — and a rushed shadda.
teacherNotes.homework: Every session opens with سَا/صَا and تَا/طَا three times each. Daily: the ص, ض, ط and ظ word sets read aloud in full; the ضِدّ self-test; the bounce-or-hold row (بَطْن — عَظْم — قُطْن — عَزْم) twice through; the four minimal-pair sets read across rather than down. Tap through both reciter rows once a day and copy the qāriʾ aloud. Finish with وَلَا ٱلضَّآلِّينَ said slowly once, counting the madd to six. Watch the ص-vs-س video and the ض-vs-ظ video once each this week.
